articles.title: When to Hire a Fractional CFO
articles.question: What changed in the company that creates a need for senior finance ownership?
articles.role: Timing trigger; keep the full role-and-fit assessment in the CFO guide.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Remove universal hours/ARR triggers and confirm embedded scope; avoid narrowing all-things-finance to strategy only.
articles.body_html:
The trigger is not ARR

Most advice frames the fractional CFO decision as a revenue milestone: hire one at $2M ARR, or after your Series A, or when you have 50 employees.

That framing is too simple. Companies at $1M ARR can have complex capital structures that require senior financial judgment. Companies at $8M ARR can have straightforward finance operations that a strong controller handles well. The trigger is the gap between the financial decisions the company faces and the financial capacity the team has.

Three signals that the gap exists

First: the founder is spending more than 10 hours a week on finance and is not good at it or does not enjoy it. That time has an opportunity cost.

Second: a board, an investor, or a lender is asking financial questions that the team cannot answer confidently without building a new spreadsheet.

Third: a capital event is approaching — a raise, a debt facility, a major contract negotiation — and the financial infrastructure underneath the company is not ready for the scrutiny.

What a fractional CFO actually does

An embedded fractional CFO is not a consultant who drops in monthly. At Centripetal, the model is 10-20 hours per week, fully embedded in the operating rhythm: cash planning, board reporting, capital decisions, scenario modeling, and the judgment calls that sit between finance and strategy.

The work is not bookkeeping. It is not tax preparation. It is the layer between the bookkeeper's output and the founder's decisions.

When to wait

If the highest-value work is processing transactions, reconciling accounts, and producing monthly close packages, the company needs a bookkeeper or controller — not a CFO. If the founder is handling finance comfortably and the board is not asking questions that stretch the team's capacity, the gap may not exist yet.

Frequently Asked Questions

At what revenue should a SaaS company hire a fractional CFO?
There is no universal revenue threshold. The trigger is the gap between the financial decisions the company faces and the financial capacity the current team has. Some companies need one at $1M ARR; others do not until much later.
What does a fractional CFO do differently than a bookkeeper?
A bookkeeper processes transactions and produces financial records. A fractional CFO provides senior financial judgment: cash planning, board reporting, capital strategy, scenario modeling, and the interpretation that connects financial data to operating decisions.
How many hours per week does a fractional CFO typically work?
Embedded fractional CFOs typically work 10-20 hours per week, integrated into the company's operating rhythm rather than visiting monthly.

articles.title: Bookkeeper, Controller, CFO: What Your Stage Actually Needs
articles.question: Which finance responsibilities are uncovered by the current team?
articles.role: Responsibility boundaries and handoffs; do not repeat the guide’s overall hiring decision.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Unverified cost multiples and workload percentages; confirm role boundaries and coordinated scope.
articles.body_html:
Three roles, three jobs

A bookkeeper processes transactions, reconciles accounts, and produces the raw financial records. A controller owns the close process, ensures the books are accurate, manages compliance, and produces reliable monthly financials. A CFO interprets the financials, makes capital decisions, builds the financial story for investors and boards, and connects financial planning to operating strategy.

These are not seniority levels. They are different jobs.

What most early-stage companies get wrong

The most common mistake is hiring a CFO when the company needs a controller. If the monthly close takes two weeks, if the chart of accounts is a mess, if revenue recognition is inconsistent, those are controller problems. A CFO will not fix them — or will fix them at 3x the cost.

The second most common mistake is expecting a bookkeeper to do controller work. A bookkeeper who also does payroll, benefits administration, and ad-hoc reporting is stretched. The work may get done, but accuracy and timeliness suffer.

How to map the work to the role

List the finance work the company actually does in a given month. Categorize each task: is it transaction processing, close and compliance, or strategy and judgment?

If 80% of the work is transaction processing, the company needs a bookkeeper. If the close and compliance layer is growing, it needs a controller. If the founder is spending meaningful time on capital decisions, board preparation, or investor conversations, it needs CFO-level judgment — which can come from a fractional CFO before a full-time hire is justified.

The fractional layer

A fractional CFO sits between the controller and a full-time CFO hire. It is the right choice when the company needs senior financial judgment but does not yet need — or cannot yet afford — a full-time finance executive.

The fractional model works when the highest-value work is strategic, not operational. When the operational finance workload grows to need a daily owner, that is when the VP Finance conversation begins.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should a startup hire a controller?
When the monthly close is unreliable, revenue recognition is inconsistent, the chart of accounts needs restructuring, or the bookkeeper is stretched beyond transaction processing into compliance and reporting work.
What is the difference between a controller and a CFO?
A controller owns accuracy: close process, compliance, and reliable financials. A CFO owns interpretation: capital decisions, board reporting, investor narrative, and connecting financial planning to operating strategy.
Can a bookkeeper handle early-stage SaaS finance?
A bookkeeper can handle transaction processing and basic reconciliation. Once the company needs reliable monthly close, revenue recognition policy, or compliance reporting, the work exceeds the bookkeeper role.

articles.title: Fractional CFO or VP Finance? The Decision Is Complexity, Not ARR
articles.question: When does daily operating ownership change the finance leadership model?
articles.role: Operating ownership and work mix; distinct from the when-to-hire timing article.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Historical pricing comparisons and assumed transition thresholds require review.
articles.body_html:
The question is usually phrased as a revenue threshold. "When should we hire a full-time CFO?" The answer founders get is often a number: $5M ARR, $10M ARR, after Series A. That is too simple. The real driver is complexity, not revenue. A $3M ARR company with a single product, one entity, and straightforward billing may not need a full-time finance executive for years. A $3M ARR company with multi-entity structure, revenue recognition complexity, debt covenants, and a board expecting institutional-grade reporting may need one yesterday.

Work Mix

The first question is what the role actually requires. At the Seed and Series A stage, the finance function typically includes: monthly close and reporting, board deck preparation, investor updates, cash flow management, financial modeling, fundraising support, and ad hoc strategic analysis. This is 10-20 hours per week of high-judgment work. A fractional CFO handles this directly. A VP Finance hire at this stage often means paying a full-time salary for part-time strategic work, with the balance filled by operational tasks that a bookkeeper or controller handles more efficiently.

Reporting Complexity

The inflection point is not revenue. It is reporting complexity. When the company has multiple entities, international operations, complex revenue recognition, or covenant compliance requirements, the daily cadence of financial management increases. A fractional CFO can handle substantial complexity, but when the role requires 30+ hours per week of consistent attention, a full-time hire becomes the right structure.

The Cost Comparison

An embedded fractional CFO typically runs $95K-$150K fully loaded per year. A VP Finance with comparable judgment and experience costs $220K-$320K loaded, before equity. The difference is not just cost. It is also the risk of a bad hire at a stage where the company cannot afford to get it wrong and start over.

When to Transition

The transition from fractional to full-time usually happens when three things converge: the weekly workload consistently exceeds 20 hours, the company needs someone managing a growing finance team, and the operating cadence requires daily cross-functional involvement. Most companies reach this point between Series A and Series B, but the timing varies with complexity, not with a specific ARR milestone.

The decision is not about what you can afford. It is about what the role actually requires. Match the structure to the work, not to a revenue benchmark that may not apply to your business.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should a SaaS company hire a VP Finance instead of a fractional CFO?
When the company needs a daily owner for a growing finance team, multi-entity reporting, covenant compliance, and recurring cross-functional operating cadence that exceeds 20 hours per week.
What does a fractional CFO cost compared to a VP Finance?
An embedded fractional CFO typically runs $95K-$150K fully loaded per year. A VP Finance with comparable judgment costs $220K-$320K loaded, before equity.
Can a fractional CFO handle board reporting and investor relations?
Yes. Board decks, investor updates, fundraising models, and cap table management are core fractional CFO work at the Seed through Series A stage.

articles.title: What AI Cannot Replace in Founder Finance
articles.question: Who checks and owns the decision supported by an AI finance output?
articles.role: Oversight and accountability; do not duplicate the Finance Scorecard’s broader diagnostic.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Replace absolute AI capability limitations and unsupported accuracy claims with specific review boundaries.
articles.body_html:
What AI does well in finance

AI is genuinely useful for transaction categorization, anomaly detection, invoice processing, expense reconciliation, and pattern recognition across large datasets. It can surface trends faster than a human scanning a spreadsheet.

For early-stage SaaS companies, this means faster bookkeeping, cleaner categorization, and more reliable data extraction from bank feeds and invoices.

Where the boundary is

The boundary is judgment. AI can tell you that your burn increased 15% this month. It cannot tell you whether that increase is a problem, a planned investment, or an artifact of timing.

It can flag that customer concentration increased. It cannot tell you whether to renegotiate the contract, diversify the pipeline, or accept the concentration as a feature of your growth stage.

It can generate a cash flow forecast from historical patterns. It cannot tell you what to do when the forecast is wrong — which it will be.

Why this matters for founders

The risk is not that AI replaces the CFO. The risk is that founders use AI outputs as a substitute for financial judgment and make decisions based on pattern recognition without the context that turns data into a decision.

A founder who relies on an AI-generated board deck without understanding what the numbers mean will not survive the first question from an institutional investor.

The practical takeaway

Use AI for data processing and pattern surfacing. Use human judgment — whether from a fractional CFO, a strong controller, or the founder's own financial literacy — for interpretation, capital decisions, board communication, and the operating responses that connect financial data to business strategy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can AI replace a fractional CFO for an early-stage startup?
No. AI can automate transaction processing and surface patterns, but it cannot provide the financial judgment needed for capital decisions, board communication, covenant management, or connecting financial data to operating strategy.
What finance tasks can AI handle for a SaaS company?
Transaction categorization, expense reconciliation, invoice processing, anomaly detection, bank feed extraction, and trend identification across historical data.
What is the risk of using AI for financial reporting?
The risk is treating pattern recognition as judgment. AI-generated outputs without human interpretation can lead to decisions based on data without context — which breaks under investor scrutiny or unexpected operating conditions.

articles.title: The Series A Data Room: What Goes In and What Gets Opened
articles.question: Can an investor trace a reported number back to its evidence?
articles.role: Evidence traceability in the data room; the guide owns the full readiness checklist.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Universal claims about document-opening sequence and investor behavior require qualification.
articles.body_html:
The data room is not a filing cabinet

Most founders treat the data room as a storage project: collect the documents, organize the folders, share the link. That is necessary but not sufficient.

The data room is a verification environment. Investors open it to test whether the numbers in the deck, the model, and the conversation all describe the same company. The order they open things in is not random.

What gets opened first

Financial statements: the most recent monthly P&L, balance sheet, and cash flow. They compare these against the numbers in the deck and model immediately.

Customer-level revenue: the schedule that shows ARR by customer, by month, for as far back as records exist. This is where concentration, churn, and expansion become visible.

Cap table: to understand the current ownership structure and how the proposed round changes it.

What gets opened during diligence

AR aging and collections history. Employment agreements and IP assignments. Debt documents, if any. Material contracts, especially the top 5-10 customer agreements. The 409A valuation. Board minutes.

These are not opened on the first day. They are opened once the investor has decided the company is interesting enough to verify.

What most founders miss

A reconciliation document. Something that explicitly maps: here is the ARR number in the deck, here is the same number in the model, here is the source data in the customer schedule, and here is how it ties to the accounting records.

If an investor has to build that bridge themselves, they will. And they will find the discrepancies you did not know were there.

Frequently Asked Questions

What documents should be in a Series A data room?
Monthly financial statements for the past 24 months, customer-level revenue by month, cap table, material contracts, employment and IP agreements, AR aging, 409A, debt documents, and a reconciliation bridge between the deck and the source data.
What do investors open first in a data room?
Financial statements, customer-level revenue schedules, and the cap table. They compare these against the numbers in the deck and the financial model to test consistency.
What do most founders miss in their data room?
A reconciliation document that explicitly maps the ARR in the deck to the customer schedule, the model, and the accounting records. Without it, investors build the bridge themselves and surface discrepancies the founder did not catch.

articles.title: What Investors Probe After Slide 12
articles.question: Which links between the pitch story and supporting evidence need explanation?
articles.role: Pitch-to-evidence reconciliation; distinguish from recurring board-reporting decisions.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Avoid universal investor behaviors, assumed deck length and deal outcomes; refine alongside Board Deck Builder.
articles.body_html:
The deck ends. The questions get more useful.

Most Series A pitch decks run ten to fifteen slides. The narrative is polished, the TAM is large, the team slide is confident. Then the deck closes and the real diligence begins. What follows is not adversarial. It is verification. And the companies that move through it quickly are the ones who anticipated the questions before they were asked.

ARR Reconciliation

Investors will ask how you define ARR and then check whether your reported number reconciles to your billing system, your accounting records, and your customer list. If those three sources tell different stories, the conversation slows down. The definition matters less than the consistency.

Customer-Level Growth

Aggregate metrics hide composition. Investors want to see revenue by customer, cohort retention, logo churn versus revenue churn, and expansion patterns. They are looking for concentration risk, dependency on a small number of accounts, and whether growth is broad-based or driven by one or two large contracts.

Forecast Decisions

A financial model is a set of decisions, not a set of predictions. Investors probe the assumptions: hiring plan, quota attainment, ramp periods, churn assumptions, expansion rates. They want to see that the forecast connects to operating decisions the team has actually made, not to aspirational growth rates copied from a benchmark report.

Cap Table Consistency

The cap table should reconcile to the legal documents. Option grants, SAFEs, convertible notes, and prior round terms should all tie out. Investors check this because surprises in the cap table create legal and economic complexity that slows or kills a deal.

Data Room Readiness

The data room is the proof layer. The deck, model, accounting records, customer data, cap table, and legal materials should reconcile without a manual translation layer. A well-organized data room signals that the company operates with the same discipline it presents in the pitch.

The pitch deck opens the conversation. The data room closes it. The distance between the two is where deals accelerate or stall.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens after a Series A pitch deck?
Investors move from narrative to verification: ARR definitions, customer-level revenue, retention, forecasts, cap table history, legal documents, and the data room.
What makes a Series A data room credible?
The deck, model, accounting records, customer data, cap table, and legal materials reconcile without a manual translation layer.
What should founders prepare beyond the pitch deck?
A metric bridge, customer-level revenue detail, a decision-ready forecast, forward-modeled ownership, and supporting corporate and financial documents.

articles.title: After the Raise, Capital Structure Becomes an Operating Decision
articles.question: How would another financing obligation change the post-raise operating plan?
articles.role: Post-raise sequencing and commitments; the debt guide owns lender/readiness evidence.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Term-dependent covenant/loan consequences and generalizations about debt timing need primary sources and qualification.
articles.body_html:
After an equity raise, venture debt is not a default next step. It is a capital structure decision with operating implications. The check has cleared, the press release is out, and the team is ready to deploy. At this point, founders often hear from lenders. The pitch is compelling: extend your runway, reduce dilution, accelerate growth. But venture debt is not free money. It comes with covenants, reporting obligations, and repayment mechanics that interact with the company's operations in ways that are not always obvious from the term sheet.

Cash Visibility

The first question is whether the company has the cash-flow visibility to support a debt obligation. Equity has no repayment schedule. Debt does. If the company's cash forecasting is not reliable enough to project debt service alongside operating expenses, the debt creates risk that outweighs the benefit.

Strong cash visibility means knowing, with reasonable precision, what the cash balance will be 6-12 months from now under multiple scenarios.

Covenant Mechanics

Venture debt typically comes with covenants: minimum cash balances, revenue milestones, reporting requirements. These are not decorative. A covenant breach triggers consequences that can range from increased reporting to acceleration of the loan.

Before signing, the company should model each covenant against its operating plan and downside scenarios. If a reasonable downside case triggers a breach, the terms need to be renegotiated or the debt should not be taken.

Sequencing

The timing of debt relative to equity matters. Debt taken immediately after an equity raise, when the balance sheet is strongest, typically gets better terms. Debt taken when the company is running low on cash and needs to bridge to the next round gets worse terms and signals distress.

The best time to negotiate debt is when you do not need it urgently.

Operating Needs vs. Headline Dilution

The decision to use debt should be driven by a specific operating need: a piece of equipment, an inventory purchase, a bridge to a known revenue milestone. "Reducing dilution" is not an operating need.

If the use of proceeds is vague, the debt is likely to create more problems than the dilution it avoids.

Capital structure is not a one-time decision made at closing. It is an ongoing operating decision that affects the company's flexibility, risk profile, and fundability. Treat it with the same rigor as any other strategic choice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should a Seed or Series A SaaS company add venture debt after raising equity?

Only if the use of proceeds is clear, the cash-flow visibility supports covenant compliance, and the debt does not create an obligation the company cannot service in a downside case.

What should founders evaluate before taking venture debt?

Cash runway with and without the debt, covenant mechanics, reporting obligations, the lender's track record with early-stage companies, and whether the capital accelerates a specific operating milestone.

How does capital structure affect the next fundraise?

Existing debt, warrant coverage, and covenant obligations are part of the investor's diligence. Clean capital structure with clear use-of-proceeds history is more fundable than maximum leverage with unclear deployment.

articles.title: The 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast: What It Shows and What It Hides
articles.question: What can a weekly cash view answer, and what depends on the longer-range plan?
articles.role: Time horizon and model boundaries; the guide owns the working forecast review.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Avoid categorical lender requirements and a universal three-scenario prescription.
articles.body_html:
What the 13-week forecast does well

A 13-week cash flow forecast shows the near-term timing of cash inflows and outflows at a weekly resolution. It makes payroll, rent, debt service, vendor payments, and expected collections visible on a calendar.

For companies with variable collection timing, seasonal patterns, or upcoming capital commitments, it is the clearest view of whether cash on hand will cover obligations over the next quarter.

What it does not show

The 13-week model is a timing instrument, not a judgment instrument. It shows when cash moves. It does not always explain which commitments are reversible, which collections are at risk, or what management would do if the downside case became the base case.

Specifically, it often hides: the distinction between committed and discretionary spend, the gap between invoiced and collected revenue, covenant trigger dates and response plans, and the decision points where management would change behavior.

How lenders read it differently

Founders build the 13-week forecast to plan operations. Lenders read it to test downside resilience.

A lender wants to know: what happens if your largest customer pays 30 days late? What happens if you move forward with a planned hire and collections slip? What is the first expense you would cut if cash dropped below a threshold?

If the model does not answer these questions, it is not lender-ready.

How to fill the gaps

Separate committed from discretionary spend. Show AR aging alongside the forecast. Add covenant triggers and response actions directly into the model. Run three scenarios — base, delayed collections, and slower growth — tied to specific management decisions.

The forecast becomes useful for capital conversations when it shows judgment, not just arithmetic.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a 13-week cash flow forecast?
A weekly projection of cash inflows and outflows over the next 13 weeks, showing when payroll, vendor payments, debt service, and expected customer collections will hit the bank account.
Why do lenders require a 13-week cash flow forecast?
Lenders use it to test whether the company can service its obligations under normal and stressed conditions. They read it for downside resilience, not just base-case timing.
What should be included beyond the basic forecast?
Committed versus discretionary spend separation, AR aging detail, covenant triggers with response actions, and three scenarios — base, delayed collections, and slower growth — tied to specific management decisions.

articles.title: Why Investors Don't Trust Your Forecast
articles.question: Can a reader follow an assumption change through the forecast to a decision?
articles.role: Assumption traceability; distinct from cash timing and invoice dependencies in the guide.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Headline and universal trust/accuracy assertions require review; no assumed investor response.
articles.body_html:
The trust problem is not accuracy

Investors do not expect the forecast to be right. They expect it to be decision-ready.

A decision-ready forecast shows what changes if a hire slips, if collections slow, if a large customer churns, or if growth comes in below plan. It connects revenue assumptions to hiring assumptions to cash assumptions to capital assumptions. When one input changes, the downstream effects are visible.

A forecast that only works in the base case is not a planning instrument. It is a wish.

Three things that break trust

First: the forecast does not tie to historical performance. If the model projects 3x growth but the last two quarters were flat, the gap between history and projection needs an explicit explanation.

Second: the forecast does not show what happens when something goes wrong. Investors will test the downside. If the model has no downside case, the investor assumes the founder has not thought about it.

Third: the assumptions are hidden. A model that shows output without making the inputs visible — hiring timeline, quota ramp, deal size assumptions, churn rate — looks like a black box.

What a credible forecast includes

Base case, upside case, and downside case — each tied to specific assumptions that can be tested. A hiring plan with costs and ramp timelines. Revenue by source (new logo, expansion, renewal) rather than a single top-line number. Cash implications of each scenario, including when the company would need to raise again or adjust spending.

The forecast should be a conversation starter, not a promise.

The Centripetal lens

A credible forecast does not predict the future. It describes the decision framework the management team is using to navigate uncertainty. Investors invest in the framework, not the prediction.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do investors distrust startup forecasts?
Usually because the forecast only works in the base case, does not tie to historical performance, hides its assumptions, or does not show what management would do if the downside case became reality.
What makes a SaaS forecast credible?
Three scenarios tied to testable assumptions, a hiring plan with costs, revenue disaggregated by source, cash implications per scenario, and a clear description of the decision framework behind the numbers.
Should a startup forecast be accurate?
Investors do not expect accuracy. They expect decision-readiness: a model that shows what changes when inputs change, and a management team that knows which levers to pull.

articles.title: Board Reporting for Seed and Series A Companies
articles.question: Which decision should the board package support at this meeting?
articles.role: Recurring board decision support; supporting resource is the broader Scorecard until the Board Deck Builder is reviewed.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Remove universal minimum cadence, generic package mandates and unsupported founder behavior assertions.
articles.body_html:
Why board reporting matters before you think it does

Most seed-stage founders treat board updates as a quarterly obligation. They send a narrative email with highlights and lowlights, maybe a few metrics.

That works until the board grows to include an institutional investor. Then the questions change. They want to reconcile the story with the numbers, see the trajectory, and understand the operating decisions behind the results. The update format that worked at three people around a kitchen table does not scale to a board with a fiduciary responsibility.

What a board package should include

A concise financial summary: revenue, burn, cash, runway. Customer health: new logos, churn, expansion, concentration. Pipeline visibility: what is in the funnel and what has changed. Hiring: plan versus actual, open roles, timeline. Key decisions: what the management team is deciding, what they need input on, and what they have already decided.

The format matters less than the consistency. A board that receives the same structure every quarter can track changes over time without re-learning the layout.

The most common mistakes

Sending too much information without highlighting what changed and what matters. Presenting metrics without context — a churn number is meaningless without the contract terms and revenue at risk. Treating the board update as a marketing document rather than a decision document. Waiting until the day before the meeting to assemble the package.

The best board packages are built incrementally throughout the quarter, not assembled in a sprint.

How to build the habit early

Start with a one-page financial summary and a one-page operating summary. Add a decision section: what you decided, what you are deciding, and what you need help with. Send it on the same day every month or quarter. Make it boring to produce — that means the data is clean and the process is repeatable.

The goal is not to impress the board. The goal is to build a reporting muscle that scales.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should a seed-stage board update include?
A concise financial summary (revenue, burn, cash, runway), customer health metrics, pipeline visibility, hiring progress, and a decisions section covering what was decided, what is being decided, and where the founder needs input.
How often should a seed-stage company send board updates?
Monthly is ideal for building the reporting habit. Quarterly is the minimum. The consistency of the cadence matters more than the frequency.
What is the most common board reporting mistake?
Treating the board update as a marketing document. The purpose is to surface decisions and build trust, not to present the company in the best possible light.

articles.title: The Cash-Flow Signals Lenders Probe That a 13-Week Model Can Hide
articles.question: Which obligations and receipt assumptions should accompany a lender cash model?
articles.role: Lender-facing evidence and obligations; do not repeat the full 13-week model explanation.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Separate lender-specific requirements from editorial review prompts; check attribution before retaining any quote.
articles.body_html:
A 13-week cash-flow model can be accurate and still leave a lender with the wrong impression.

The reason is simple: a weekly cash view tells you when cash moves. It does not always explain which commitments are reversible, which collections are fragile, or what happens when a covenant is tested.

This is the lender's lens looking into your books.

Start with committed versus discretionary spend

Separate payroll, rent, debt service, contracted vendors, and other obligations you cannot quickly remove from discretionary hiring, projects, and vendors you can pause. Two companies with the same weekly burn can have very different room to maneuver.

A lender wants to know what happens if collections arrive late or a planned hire moves forward. If every expense is treated as equally flexible, the model hides the real downside.

Make collection lag visible

Cash flow should show the difference between invoiced revenue and collected cash. Review AR aging, payment terms, renewal timing, and the customers that account for a meaningful share of open receivables.

A model that assumes every invoice converts on schedule is not conservative. It is incomplete.

For SaaS companies with annual contracts, the question is not only how much ARR exists. It is when the cash arrives, what sits behind it, and what changes if one large customer pays late.

Map covenant and runway triggers

Do not wait until a lender sends a covenant schedule. Put the triggers in the operating model: minimum cash, reporting dates, revenue or performance tests, borrowing-base mechanics where relevant, and the actions management would take if a threshold is approached.

The useful question is not “How many months of runway do we have?” It is “What decision changes first if the downside case becomes the base case?”

Run three views, not one

Use a base case, a delayed-collections case, and a slower-growth case. Tie each to specific actions: pause a hiring cohort, renegotiate a vendor, reduce discretionary spend, or revisit the capital plan.

The model becomes lender-ready when it shows judgment, not just arithmetic.

The Centripetal lens

A 13-week model is a useful instrument. It is not the whole cash story. Lenders are looking for the structure behind the number: what is committed, what is collectible, what is covenant-sensitive, and what management will do next.

For the broader debt-readiness package, see our Venture Debt Readiness Checklist. For post-close operating discipline, see The First 90 Days After Your Raise.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a 13-week cash-flow model enough for venture debt diligence?
No. It should be paired with committed-spend analysis, AR collection assumptions, covenant triggers, existing obligations, and downside scenarios tied to management actions.
What cash-flow detail do lenders often question first?
The gap between invoiced revenue and collected cash, especially when a small number of customers represent a meaningful share of open receivables.
How should a SaaS company prepare for a covenant discussion?
Put minimum cash, reporting dates, performance tests, and response actions directly into the operating model before the lender asks for them.

articles.title: Treasury Controls Every SaaS Founder Should Have Before the Next Board Meeting
articles.question: Can the team demonstrate who can move cash and how exceptions are checked?
articles.role: Control ownership and evidence; the guide owns the wider treasury review.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: FDIC/product coverage mechanics, 30-minute promises and universal controls need review.
articles.body_html:
Why treasury is not a later-stage problem

Most early-stage SaaS founders do not think about treasury until something forces them to: a bank failure makes the news, an auditor asks about FDIC coverage, or a board member asks who has signatory authority.

The truth is that treasury controls are straightforward to set up and easy to neglect. A 30-minute review can surface risks that would otherwise go unnoticed until they become expensive.

The five controls that matter

Bank structure: are operating funds and reserve funds separated? If all cash sits in one account, a single fraud event or bank issue affects everything.

FDIC coverage: does the company's cash exceed the $250,000 per-depositor insurance limit? If so, is there a sweep arrangement or a second banking relationship?

Signatory controls: who can authorize payments, wire transfers, and account changes? If one person can move all the company's cash without a second approval, that is a control gap.

Sweep mechanics: is excess cash earning yield in a money market or treasury fund, or is it sitting in a zero-interest checking account?

Fraud prevention: are ACH and wire controls in place? Is positive pay enabled? Are payment thresholds set for dual approval?

How to do the review

Take 30 minutes. Pull up each bank account. Check the balance against the FDIC limit. Verify the authorized signers. Check whether sweep or yield is enabled. Confirm the fraud prevention controls.

Document the answers. If anything is missing, fix it. This is not a quarterly project — it is a one-time setup with an annual check.

When the board asks

The next time a board member asks about treasury controls, the right answer is: here is our bank structure, here is our FDIC coverage, here are the authorized signers, here are the fraud controls, and here is when we last reviewed them.

That answer takes 30 minutes to prepare. Not having it takes longer to explain.

Frequently Asked Questions

What treasury controls should an early-stage SaaS company have?
Separated operating and reserve accounts, FDIC coverage awareness with sweep or multi-bank arrangements if cash exceeds $250K, dual-signatory controls, fraud prevention (positive pay, ACH blocks, wire thresholds), and a documented review date.
How long does a treasury review take?
About 30 minutes for the initial review: check each bank account balance against FDIC limits, verify authorized signers, confirm sweep and fraud controls, and document the results. Annual re-checks take less.
When should a startup worry about FDIC coverage?
As soon as any single bank account holds more than $250,000. This often happens shortly after a fundraise, when the full amount is deposited into one operating account.

articles.title: CARR vs ARR: When the Definition Matters
articles.question: Which definition and contract timing explain the gap between contracted and live recurring revenue?
articles.role: Metric definition bridge; do not become a generic ARR glossary or repeat diligence checklist.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: ARR is not recognized accounting revenue; remove unsupported 1–2% tolerance and verify contract/activation treatment.
articles.body_html:
Why the distinction matters

ARR measures what is live and recognized. CARR measures what is contracted, including deals signed but not yet live. When an investor asks for ARR, they are asking for the tighter number. When a founder reports CARR as ARR, the reconciliation breaks in diligence.

This is not a semantic issue. The gap between CARR and ARR is an implementation timeline, a revenue-recognition policy, and a credibility test. A clean answer requires knowing which number you are reporting, what the difference is, and when the difference closes.

Where the gap shows up

The gap is usually largest in companies with longer implementation cycles, multi-product upsells with staged rollouts, or contracts where billing starts before the customer is fully live.

When an investor sees ARR in the deck and a different number in the financial model or accounting export, the first question is whether the founder is using the same definition across all three. If the answer requires a spreadsheet that maps contracts to go-live dates, the data room needs that spreadsheet before the first partner meeting.

How to present both numbers

Report ARR as the primary metric. Report CARR as a secondary metric with an explicit bridge: which contracts are signed but not yet live, what the expected go-live timeline is, and what the historical conversion rate from signed to live has been.

Investors do not penalize companies for having a CARR-to-ARR gap. They penalize companies for not knowing the gap exists or for presenting the larger number without context.

The reconciliation test

Take your ARR number from the deck. Compare it to the ARR number in the financial model. Compare both to the recurring revenue line in the P&L. Compare all three to the customer-level revenue schedule.

If all four match within 1-2%, you have clean ARR. If they do not match, the work is not to adjust the slide. The work is to clean the definition, build the bridge, and document the policy.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between CARR and ARR?
CARR is contracted annual recurring revenue, including deals signed but not yet live. ARR is annual recurring revenue from contracts that are live, recognized, and generating revenue. The gap is the implementation pipeline.
Should I report CARR or ARR to investors?
Report ARR as the primary number. Show CARR as a secondary metric with a clear bridge explaining the contracts in implementation and their expected go-live timeline.
How do investors test whether ARR is accurate?
They compare the ARR in the deck to the number in the model, the accounting records, and the customer-level revenue schedule. If the number differs across any of these, they ask why.

articles.title: Customer Concentration: The Board Question You Should Answer First
articles.question: What operating decision changes if a material customer renews late or leaves?
articles.role: Customer dependency and contract exposure; the guide owns the broader cash review.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Remove universal concentration thresholds and investor-order claims; distinguish ARR share from weekly receipt dependence.
articles.body_html:
Why concentration matters more than founders expect

Customer concentration is the first thing most investors check after ARR. Not because concentration is inherently bad, but because the implications change depending on how the founder understands it.

A company where 40% of revenue comes from two accounts is not automatically uninvestable. But a company where the founder cannot explain why those two accounts are sticky, what the renewal terms look like, and what happens to the P&L if one churns — that company has a concentration problem.

What investors actually probe

They will ask for the top 1, top 5, and top 10 customer revenue shares. They will ask about contract length, renewal timing, pricing structure, and whether the largest customers were acquired through the same channel as the rest of the base.

The deeper question is whether concentration is a feature of the growth stage (early companies naturally have concentration) or a structural dependency the company has not diversified away from.

How to frame it honestly

If concentration is high, own it. Show the renewal history. Show the expansion revenue from those accounts. Show what the pipeline looks like for new logos that would reduce the ratio over the next 12 months.

The worst answer is a slide that minimizes the number. The second worst answer is a plan to reduce concentration that does not have a realistic timeline.

The board-level question

The question for the board is not 'is our concentration too high?' It is 'if our largest customer churned tomorrow, what would we do?' If the answer is clear and the team has modeled the scenario, concentration is a known risk. If the answer requires a pause, it is an unmanaged risk.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a concerning level of customer concentration for SaaS?
There is no universal threshold. Investors probe concentration relative to contract length, renewal visibility, and the company's pipeline for new logos. A 30% top-customer share with a 3-year contract is different from 30% with month-to-month billing.
How should a founder present customer concentration to investors?
Show the top 1, 5, and 10 customer revenue shares. Include contract terms, renewal dates, and expansion history. Frame the path to diversification with a realistic timeline.
What board question does customer concentration answer?
If our largest customer churned tomorrow, what would we do — and have we modeled that scenario? The answer determines whether concentration is a known risk or an unmanaged one.

articles.title: The Vertical SaaS Advantage Has a Half-Life
articles.question: How does the acquisition plan change as growth moves beyond founder-led distribution?
articles.role: Channel mix and repeatability; belongs to finance operations/growth metrics without a new top-level category.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Avoid universal CAC trajectories and unsupported market patterns; validate sophistication and actual Centripetal scope.
articles.body_html:
Vertical SaaS founders often begin with a distribution edge. They know the industry. They know the buyers. They speak the language. Early customers come through relationships, conferences, and word of mouth. CAC is low. Payback is fast. The unit economics look exceptional.

The question is how long it lasts.

The Initial Advantage

In the early stages, vertical SaaS companies often acquire customers at a fraction of the cost of horizontal competitors. The founder's network is the distribution channel. Industry credibility replaces brand awareness. Referrals replace paid acquisition.

This is a real advantage, and it shows up in the metrics: lower CAC, faster sales cycles, higher win rates. But it is important to understand what is driving those numbers. If the advantage is the founder's personal network, it is inherently limited by the size of that network.

Maturation Dynamics

As the company grows past the founder's immediate network, acquisition dynamics shift. The easy customers have already been reached. The next tier requires outbound sales, content marketing, paid channels, or partnerships. Each of these costs more than a warm introduction.

CAC begins to rise. Sales cycles lengthen. The metrics start to look more like a horizontal SaaS company, because the distribution mechanics are converging.

Measuring the Edge

The way to track this is straightforward: measure blended CAC, channel-specific CAC, and payback period by quarter. Compare the founder-led channel against paid and inbound. The gap between them is the advantage. The trend over time is the half-life.

If the founder-led channel is shrinking as a share of new revenue while blended CAC is rising, the advantage is decaying. This is not a problem if the company is building durable distribution channels alongside the founder's network. It is a problem if the entire growth plan depends on the initial edge persisting.

Extending the Advantage

The companies that sustain low CAC in vertical markets do so by converting the founder's initial credibility into institutional assets: a recognized brand within the vertical, a content engine that generates inbound, product features that create switching costs, and a customer base that generates referrals without the founder's direct involvement.

The goal is to make the distribution advantage a property of the company, not a property of the founder.

The Bottom Line

A vertical SaaS distribution advantage is real and valuable. It is also finite unless the company invests in making it durable. Track the half-life. Build the replacement channels before the initial edge erodes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does vertical SaaS create a lasting customer-acquisition advantage?
It creates an initial advantage. The durability depends on whether the founder's network and credibility translate into a repeatable, measurable distribution channel -- or remain informal.
How should a vertical SaaS company measure its distribution advantage?
Track blended CAC, channel-specific CAC, and payback period by quarter. Compare the founder-led channel against paid and inbound. The gap is the advantage; the trend is the half-life.
What happens when the reachable vertical market matures?
CAC converges toward horizontal SaaS benchmarks. The company needs either deeper product moats, adjacent verticals, or a platform strategy before the initial edge erodes.
